definitions.definition: A transmission technique where the signal bandwidth is made much greater than the message bandwidth, using a spreading code independent of the message.
A deterministic binary code that appears random, generated by an LFSR with primitive-polynomial feedback; an n-stage register produces a sequence of length 2^n.
PN-sequence property that over one period the number of ones and zeros differs by at most one, with ones exactly one more than zeros.
PN characteristic that about half of all stretches of identical bits have length 1, a quarter length 2, an eighth length 3, and 2^-n length n.
PN-property that comparing any cyclic shift of a sequence with itself, the number of agreements differs from the number of disagreements by at most one, easing synchronization.
A set of 2^n + 1 sequences of period 2^n − 1 formed from a preferred pair of m-sequences, with small bounded cross-correlations; used in CDMA and GPS.
A set of 2^(m/2) sequences of period 2^m − 1 generated for even m from two m-sequences, in a fashion similar to Gold-code generation.
A mutually orthogonal ±1 sequence obtained by selecting a row of a Hadamard matrix, with larger sets built by the Hadamard recursion.
Specially designed binary sequence with almost ideal aperiodic autocorrelation; its time-reversed form is also such a sequence, and no longer ones exist.
A tree-ordered orthogonal code set (same set as Walsh-Hadamard, different order) where a code can be assigned only if no ancestor or descendant code is already in use.
M-ary modulation with n = 3, in which tribits are encoded into eight output phases with 45° spacing and minimum bandwidth equal to fb/3.
Modulation that conveys data by changing (not setting) the carrier phase relative to the previous phase, overcoming phase-rotation ambiguity of plain BPSK/QPSK.
Spread-spectrum scheme in which each data bit is XOR-combined with a spreading code, expanding the signal across a wider band in proportion to the code length.
Spread-spectrum multiplexing where each user's bits are broken into chips by a fixed user-specific code, so a decoder knowing the code ignores other users.
A DS-CDMA diversity receiver whose separate correlators (fingers) each lock to a resolvable multipath component delayed by at least one chip, with weighted combination forming the bit decision.
A CDMA impairment where interference from a user near the base station overpowers the weaker signal from a distant user.
A CDMA feature where a mobile is simultaneously connected to two or more cells or sectors during a call; same-site sectors give softer handoff.

A detection approach that exploits the other users' spreading codes instead of treating multi-access interference as AWGN, increasing system capacity beyond the matched-filter approach (Verdu's optimum detector).
The fixed wired telephone network exchanging information over trunks of fiber, copper, microwave or satellite links.
Network protocol standard enabling automatic (autonomous) roaming, allowing MSCs of different service providers to pass subscriber information (via HLR/VLR) to other MSCs on demand.
A second-generation wireless-network handoff technique in which the mobile station reports received power and scans adjacent base stations to assist the handoff decision.
Routing where the MSC dedicates a voice channel between base station and PSTN for the entire call.

A connectionless service that breaks each message into packets carrying a header (source, destination, sequence and routing information) and a trailer (cyclic redundancy checksum for error detection).
A widely used CCITT (ITU-T) packet standard that is a common interface in the lower three layers.
A packet data service for early US cellular systems that overlays existing infrastructure and occupies voice channels on a secondary, non-interfering basis.
A digital communications technique providing simultaneous transmission of user data, signaling data and related traffic over a separate out-of-band signaling channel.
The ISDN-defined protocol family used for CCS between interconnected networks; its lowest three layers form the network service part (NSP), made up of MTP and SCCP.
A set of digital communication standards for phone, video and data calls over traditional PSTN circuits, offering BRI (2 B-channels + 1 D-channel) and PRI interfaces.
Wide-capacity extension of the digital telephone standard based on asynchronous transfer mode, supporting packet switching for high-capacity computer and video-imaging applications.
A family of wired computer networking technologies used in LANs, MANs and WANs, commercially introduced in 1980 and first standardized in 1983 as IEEE 802.3.
A communication protocol created by extending IP that lets a user move between networks keeping the same IP address, built on three capabilities: discovery, registration and tunneling.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: The Mobile IP procedure in which a mobile node identifies prospective home and foreign agents from periodic ICMP router advertisements with Mobile-IP-specific extensions.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: The tunnel exit point of Mobile IP forwarding; either the foreign agent's IP address or a co-located address on the mobile node's interface.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: An authenticated four-step procedure in which the mobile node, via the foreign agent, alerts its home agent to forward its IP traffic to the newly acquired care-of address.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: Forwarding of IP datagrams from a home address to a care-of address by placing the entire datagram as payload of an outer IP datagram.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: A Mobile IP encapsulation option (RFC 2004) inserting an 8-octet forwarding header between the original IP header and payload.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: An application-layer protocol that initiates and terminates IP communication sessions for voice, messaging and video; endpoints are identified by an email address, IP address or phone number.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: Universal, open standard from the industry forum giving portable phones and terminals access to telephony and Internet information services on all network technologies.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: An XML-adhering markup language for presenting content on limited-bandwidth, small-screen, limited-input devices using a deck/card organizational metaphor.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: A transaction-oriented request/reply protocol whose PDUs carry a body (WML, WMLScript or images) plus a header, with capability negotiation, session suspend/resume and server push.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: A lightweight, operation-oriented reliable transport standard that dispenses with TCP overhead, suitable for thin clients over low-bandwidth links, with three classes.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: The WAP layer that adapts higher WAP protocols to the bearer used between the mobile node and the gateway, hiding bearer details and providing bearer-independent segmentation and reassembly.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: The successor to IPv4 designed to overcome address exhaustion, using 128-bit colon-hex addresses, with unicast/multicast/anycast types, a simplified header and stateless address autoconfiguration.
definitions.unitTitle: Mobile IP and Wireless Access Protocol

definitions.definition: Network name that an access point announces in beacon frames and that a station names in its association request.
WLAN amendment using the 2.4 GHz band at up to 11 Mbit/s raw rate with DSSS and CCK modulation.
WLAN amendment using the 2.4 GHz band with OFDM for up to 54 Mbit/s and backward compatibility with the 11 Mbit/s standard.
WLAN amendment using the 5 GHz band with OFDM modulation for a raw rate of up to 54 Mbit/s.
WLAN amendment using MIMO-OFDM with up to 64-QAM in the 2.4 and 5 GHz bands for rates up to about 600 Mbit/s.
5 GHz-only WLAN amendment using wide channels up to 160 MHz and up to 256-QAM for multi-gigabit rates.
Medium access method where a station listens to the channel before each frame, optionally exchanging RTS and CTS to handle hidden stations.
ETSI 5 GHz wireless LAN standard using OFDM with dynamic TDMA access and quality-of-service support, with a physical layer similar to 802.11a.
Overlay that extends a private network across a public one such as the internet, using encryption and tunneling.
Short-range wireless standard for exchanging data between devices over about ten metres, standardised by the IEEE as 802.15.1.
Small ad hoc network in which one master device communicates with up to seven active slaves that all follow the master's clock.
Interconnection of two or more small master-slave networks in which some device is master in one and slave in another.
Radio technique sending each packet on one of 79 one-megahertz channels, about 1,600 hops per second, with adaptive hopping to avoid crowded frequencies.
Software on the device's processor that sets up, authenticates and configures connections between Bluetooth devices using LMP.
Part of the Bluetooth digital controller that handles baseband processing, error correction and retransmission, audio coding and encryption.
Family of wireless broadband standards based on IEEE 802.16, which defines both the physical layer and the MAC layer.
Medium access design of 802.16 in which a base station assigns each subscriber station a fixed time slot, unlike contention-based CSMA/CA.
Device such as a handset, USB dongle or laptop module that connects to a WiMAX base station.
Multicarrier scheme sending data over closely spaced orthogonal subcarriers so that they do not interfere and need no guard bands.
Copy of the end of each symbol sent ahead of it in the guard interval, so multipath echoes cause no intersymbol interference.
Ratio of peak to average transmitted power, high in multicarrier signals because independent subcarriers often add constructively, demanding linear power amplifiers.
Wireless technique using several transmit and receive antennas to raise link capacity through spatial diversity and spatial multiplexing.
Splitting a high-rate stream into several lower-rate streams sent simultaneously on the same frequency and separated by their spatial signatures.
Only network element on the radio access side of LTE's E-UTRAN, serving the mobile devices directly.
Key control node of the LTE core handling paging, bearer setup, gateway selection, NAS signalling and user authentication with the subscriber database.
Time-division variant of LTE in which uplink and downlink share one frequency channel.
Industry-standardised method of carrying voice calls over LTE using the IP multimedia subsystem, typically with a wideband AMR codec.
